title: Ὀρνιθοθήρας καὶ πελαργός
part: The Fowler and the Stork (Chambry 284 · Perry 194)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 284 (= Perry 194). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὀρνιθοθήρας δίκτυα γεράνοις ἀναπετάσας πόρρωθεν ἀπεκαραδόκει τὴν ἄγραν.
sentences.tr: Ornithothēras diktya geranois anapetasas porrōthen apekaradokei tēn agran.
sentences.l: A fowler, having spread out nets for cranes, watched from a distance for the catch.
sentences.n: ἀποκαραδοκέω is to crane the head forward and watch for something intently — the same verb, in the same posture, opens fable 282. Cranes come down in flocks onto sown fields, which is why the nets are set for them.

sentences.t: Πελαργοῦ δὲ σὺν ταῖς γεράνοις ἐπικαθίσαντος, ἐπιδραμὼν μετ’ ἐκείνων καὶ αὐτὸν συνέλαβε.
sentences.tr: Pelargou de syn tais geranois epikathisantos, epidramōn met’ ekeinōn kai auton synelabe.
sentences.l: And when a stork had settled down along with the cranes, he ran up and took him too along with them.
sentences.n: γέρανος is feminine in Greek, as ταῖς shows, though the stork is masculine — the genders are the birds' grammatical genders and carry no sense here.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ δεομένου μεθεῖναι αὐτὸν καὶ λέγοντος ὡς οὐ μόνον αὐτὸς ἀβλαβής ἐστι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὠφελιμώτατος, τοὺς γὰρ ὄφεις καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἑρπετὰ συλλαμβάνων κατεσθίει, ὁ ὀρνιθοθήρας ἀπεκρίνατο· « Ἀλλ’ εἰ τὰ μάλιστα μὴ φαῦλος σὺ εἶ, δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο γοῦν ἄξιος εἶ κολάσεως, ὅτι μετὰ πονηρῶν κεκάθικας. »
sentences.tr: Tou de deomenou metheinai auton kai legontos hōs ou monon autos ablabēs esti tois anthrōpois, alla kai ōphelimōtatos, tous gar opheis kai ta loipa herpeta syllambanōn katesthiei, ho ornithothēras apekrinato· « All’ ei ta malista mē phaulos sy ei, di’ auto touto goun axios ei kolaseōs, hoti meta ponērōn kekathikas. »
sentences.l: And when he begged him to let him go, and said that he is not only himself harmless to men but even most useful — for, taking the snakes and the rest of the creeping things, he eats them up — the fowler answered: « But even if you are in the highest degree not bad, for this very thing at any rate you are worthy of punishment, because you have taken your seat among the wicked. »
sentences.i: And the stork begged him to let him go, saying that he was not merely harmless to men but useful in the highest degree, since he takes snakes and the other creeping things and eats them; but the fowler answered: « Even granting that you are no bad bird, for that very reason you deserve punishment: you have taken your seat among the wicked. »
sentences.n: ὡς after λέγοντος introduces reported speech, and the tense of the direct words is kept unchanged (ἐστι, κατεσθίει) — Greek does not shift tenses back as English does. The γάρ clause is the stork's own supporting reason, still inside the report. εἰ τὰ μάλιστα is 'granted it to the utmost', a concession made for argument's sake. κεκάθικας is a perfect: not 'you sat down' but 'you have sat down and are sitting there', which is the whole of the fowler's charge.

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς δεῖ τὰς τῶν πονηρῶν συνηθείας περιφεύγειν, ἵνα μὴ καὶ αὐτοὶ τῆς ἐκείνων κακίας κοινωνεῖν δόξωμεν.
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas dei tas tōn ponērōn synētheias peripheugein, hina mē kai autoi tēs ekeinōn kakias koinōnein doxōmen.
sentences.l: So then we too must shun the company of the wicked, so that we ourselves may not seem to share in their badness.
sentences.n: κοινωνέω takes the genitive of the thing shared in. περιφεύγειν is 'flee all round', hence to keep well clear of — the same verb closes fable 60, likewise about the company one keeps.
